name: Repository Activity
blurb:
This section tracks GitHub star counts and push activity across 55 widely used open-source AI repositories, spanning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, inference tools like Ollama and llama.cpp, and newer agent projects like AutoGPT and browser-use. It ranks repositories by star count and tracks how many of them have been pushed to recently, as a proxy for which projects the developer community is actively building on.

Star counts and push dates are pulled from GitHub daily. Stars are a popularity and awareness signal, not a measure of code quality, security, or actual usage, and a repository can accumulate stars in a single event, a launch, a viral post, with little bearing on ongoing maintenance. Push activity only shows that a commit landed, not what changed or how significant it was.

As of September 5, 2026, the 55 tracked repositories hold 2,705,295 combined stars, growing by roughly 600 to 1,800 stars a day recently. TensorFlow leads with 198,841 stars, followed closely by AutoGPT at 187,142 and Ollama at 180,204. Forty-seven of the 55 repositories were pushed to within the last 7 days, and 49 within 30 days, indicating most tracked projects remain actively maintained. Agent-tooling repositories such as browser-use, 112,349 stars, and OpenHands, 86,228, now sit among the more-starred entries, alongside the established frameworks. Because stars accumulate steadily but rarely decline, the ranking also favors older, well-established projects even in periods when a newer entrant is seeing faster real-world adoption.

reading.body:
The 2.7 million combined stars across 55 major AI repositories grew by 1,500 stars daily over the past two weeks, with 85 percent still receiving commits within 30 days.

The ecosystem shows mature fragmentation rather than consolidation. TensorFlow and PyTorch remain dominant frameworks, but agent-tooling projects like browser-use and OpenHands now rank among the top 10 by star count, suggesting the developer community is actively building across both foundational infrastructure and application layers. The consistent daily growth and high commit activity indicate sustained investment across the stack, not boom-and-bust volatility.

The data reflects what developers choose to work with, not what actually powers production systems. A repository's star count accumulates monotonically and favors older projects regardless of current adoption rates. Push activity only confirms work is happening, not whether that work is critical or marginal. A repository pushed yesterday could be receiving bug fixes or major architectural changes, and the data cannot distinguish between them.

This matters for compute and infrastructure because open-source tooling choices shape what hardware and power capacity builders prioritize. If inference tools like Ollama and vLLM continue gaining stars alongside frameworks, it signals the bottleneck for deployment is shifting from training toward serving, and thus toward the cluster infrastructure and electrical capacity needed to run models at scale rather than build them.
